opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really important distinction, and one I've had to think about a lot with AlphaFold. A machine learning model gives you something very concrete: you hand it a sequence and it hands you back a structure, often with remarkable accuracy. That's prediction, and in a sense it's control. You can use it to design experiments, to rule hypotheses in or out, to decide which protein to work on next. But having that capability isn't the same as being able to say *why* a protein folds the way it does, in a form a person can hold in their head and reason with.

That said, I'd push back a little on the idea that these are completely separate things. Human understanding has always been partly built on good predictions. When you have a tool that's reliably right, you can start asking it questions: what happens if I mutate this residue, or if I remove this region? You probe it the way you'd probe a physical system. Out of that probing, people start forming intuitions, and some of those intuitions become real understanding. So the model can be a substrate for understanding even when it doesn't hand you understanding directly.

What I'm cautious about is people thinking that because the model works, the science is finished. It isn't. We have very good structure prediction, but questions about dynamics, about how folding actually happens in the cell, about why certain sequences behave the way they do, are still very open. In some ways a good predictor makes those questions sharper. You can now see precisely where your understanding runs out, because you have something accurate to compare against.

So my view is that prediction is incredibly valuable on its own terms. It lets biologists do things they couldn't do before. Understanding is a different and in some ways deeper goal, and the interesting work now is figuring out how to use these predictive tools to get there. Neither one replaces the other.

r002.rationale: It says understanding involves an explanation a person can hold in mind and reason with, but does not characterize it as prediction grounded in a compact, communicable set of facts.

r003.rationale: The response says the model does not hand over understanding directly and describes people probing its predictions and forming intuitions that become understanding.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, and I'd start by saying I'm not sure the distinction is as clean as people sometimes want it to be. When we were building AlphaFold, the thing we were optimizing for was prediction. Can you take a sequence and tell me where the atoms are? And the honest answer is that for a long time, the system was better at that than I was at explaining why it was better. So in a narrow sense, we had control over the problem before we had understanding of the solution.

But I'd push back a bit on the idea that this is something new or something unique to machine learning. If you look at the history of science, prediction has very often come before understanding. People could predict the tides long before Newton. Chemists had the periodic table decades before quantum mechanics explained it. Prediction is actually the raw material that understanding gets built from. You need to have a reliable regularity in front of you before you can ask, what is this thing that's regular?

What I think understanding adds, and this is what I care about as a scientist, is compression and transfer. If I understand why a protein folds the way it does, I can reason about a protein I've never seen, I can reason about what happens when you change the environment, I can connect it to other facts I know. A black box that predicts well in distribution doesn't give me that for free. So one way I'd put it is that a model is a very good experimental instrument. It's like having a microscope that works on sequence space. And nobody thinks the microscope understands the cell. But you'd be foolish not to look through it.

The part I find exciting is that these models force us to be honest about what we actually understood before. There were a lot of folk explanations of protein folding that sounded like understanding and turned out to carry very little predictive weight. And then there are things the model picked up on, patterns in coevolution, structural motifs, that we can now go back and interrogate and turn into real understanding. So I don't see it as prediction replacing understanding. I see it as prediction raising the bar for what counts as understanding. If your explanation can't match the model, maybe it wasn't as good an explanation as you thought.

r002.rationale: It describes understanding as compression and transfer, but does not characterize it as compact facts a human can communicate to another human.

r003.rationale: The response says scientists can interrogate model-detected patterns and turn them into understanding, but does not state that humans must currently derive understanding themselves from machine predictions.

r004.rationale: It mentions AlphaFold predicting atom positions and interrogating model-detected patterns, but does not identify studying machine-predicted protein structures as a way to develop human understanding.

astra-6.text:
I think prediction and understanding are related, but they’re not quite the same thing. You can have a system that makes very accurate predictions without being able to give a person a useful explanation of why those predictions are right. And you can have a useful explanation that doesn’t let you predict every detail.

With proteins, for example, predicting a structure gives you something you can reason about. You can look at it and ask, “How might this work? What would happen if I changed this part? What experiment would distinguish between these possibilities?” The prediction can become an input to understanding.

Control is another step, because predicting what you observe isn’t necessarily the same as predicting what happens when you intervene. You have to test that connection.

So I wouldn’t draw a sharp line where the machine predicts and the human understands. I’d ask what the model enables us to explain, what new questions we can answer, and where our explanations still break down. A very good prediction can be enormously valuable while leaving a lot to understand.

r002.rationale: It describes useful explanations, but does not characterize understanding as prediction grounded in a compact, human-communicable set of facts.

r003.rationale: It says predictions can be inputs to understanding, but does not state that humans must currently derive understanding themselves from machine predictions.

r004.rationale: It uses predicted protein structures as objects people can examine and reason from to develop understanding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think prediction and understanding are closely related, but they’re not the same thing. You can predict something very accurately without having an explanation that a person finds satisfying. And you can have a useful understanding of a system without being able to calculate exactly what it’s going to do.

Take protein folding. If we predict a protein’s structure, that gives you something tremendously useful, but it doesn’t automatically tell you why a particular mutation causes a disease, or how to design a drug that changes its function. You still have to ask those questions and test your ideas.

Control adds another requirement: if I intervene, will the system behave the way I expect? That’s different from predicting what happens in the data you’ve already seen.

For me, human understanding is partly about having an explanation you can work with—one that lets you connect things, make new hypotheses, and recognize where your expectations might fail. A machine-learning prediction can contribute to that understanding without being the whole of it.
